anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Tables, indexes, partitions, constraints, or data types are not aligned with workload access patterns, forcing the optimizer into unnecessarily wide scans and non-covering lookups regardless of statistics or parameter settings.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical disks or storage subsystem are unable to sustain the read/write throughput, IOPS, or latency demanded by the database, producing long device queues and I/O waits even when the database engine is correctly configured.

When both root causes strike together, the workload generates an excessive volume of physical I/O because of missing or sub-optimal indexes, large table scans, and extra row fetches, while the underlying storage cannot absorb this load. Symptoms include: execution plans that fall back to full scans or repeated bookmark lookups, buffer cache churn, and spill-to-temp operations; concurrent surges in data-file, temp-space, and log-flush waits; device queue depths pinned high with service times that grow non-linearly; CPU utilization oscillating between idle (waiting on I/O) and spikes during short bursts of work; dramatic, workload-wide latency variability where individual statements appear to "hang" and batch or ETL windows overrun.

Causally, inadequate schema and index design magnifies the volume of physical reads and writes, quickly pushing the storage subsystem past its sustainable bandwidth. Once disks are saturated, I/O latency lengthens, which in turn makes the inefficient access paths even more expensive, causing the optimizer to favor still broader scans or additional spilling, thereby further compounding the load. The intertwined feedback loop means that neither redesigning storage tiers nor merely adding indexes alone will fully resolve performance issues; both the data model and the storage capacity must be addressed together to restore stable and predictable performance.

entry.official_description: Schema '%.192s' does not exist, but schema directory '%.192s' was found. This must be resolved manually (e.g. by moving the schema directory to another location).
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with file creation, filesystem access, write durability, log persistence, tablespace management, or storage-capacity boundaries.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect filesystem capacity and permissions, verify persistence paths, review log and data placement, and check whether storage latency or write failures are affecting the engine.
